Phishing

Messages designed to trick users into revealing information or clicking malicious links.

🔑

Credential Attacks

🔗

Suspicious Links

🔐

Password Security

📱

MFA

🧠

Social Engineering

👁️

Data Privacy

Limit unnecessary sharing of personal and sensitive information.

🦠

Malware

STRIDE FRAMEWORK

Threat Model

This threat model identifies potential threats to PhishAware and shows where security controls can reduce risk.

👤 UserCredential & authentication attacks
↓
🌐 Web BrowserCross-Site Scripting (XSS)
↓
🖥️ Web ServerDenial-of-Service
↓
⚙️ ApplicationAuthorization & unauthorized access
↓
🗄️ DatabaseSQL injection & data leakage

Potential Security Threats

HIGH

Authentication Attacks

Attackers may attempt to access accounts using compromised credentials.

Mitigation: MFA, strong password policies, rate limiting.
HIGH

Authorization Attacks

Users may attempt to access resources outside their permitted role.

Mitigation: Server-side authorization checks and least privilege.
HIGH

SQL Injection

Malicious input may attempt to manipulate database queries.

Mitigation: Parameterized queries and input validation.
HIGH

Cross-Site Scripting

Untrusted content may attempt to execute scripts in a browser.

Mitigation: Output encoding, sanitization, and CSP.
MEDIUM

Denial-of-Service

Excessive requests may reduce application availability.

Mitigation: Rate limiting and traffic monitoring.
HIGH

Credential Attacks

Stolen or reused credentials can be used to access accounts.

Mitigation: MFA and credential protections.
HIGH

Data Leakage

Sensitive information could be exposed through insecure handling.

Mitigation: Encryption, access control, and minimal data collection.
HIGH

Unauthorized Access

An attacker may attempt to reach protected resources.

Mitigation: Authentication, authorization, logging.

STRIDE Analysis

S — Spoofing

Pretending to be another user. Protect with strong authentication and MFA.

T — Tampering

Unauthorized data changes. Protect with validation and integrity controls.

R — Repudiation

Denying an action occurred. Protect with appropriate audit logging.

I — Information Disclosure

Exposure of confidential data. Protect with encryption and access controls.

D — Denial of Service

Making services unavailable. Protect with rate limiting and monitoring.

E — Elevation of Privilege

Gaining excessive permissions. Protect with least privilege and authorization checks.

ASSIGNMENT 3 · SECURE WEB ARCHITECTURE

Designing a Secure PhishAware Platform

How PhishAware works today, and how its architecture would evolve into a secure, account-based phishing analysis service.

CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION

Static educational website

GitHub Pages serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images over HTTPS. The quiz, chatbot, and phishing analyzer run in the visitor's browser. There is no custom backend, database, login, or server-side session today.

PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE

Secure full-stack expansion

A dedicated web/API server would support user accounts, server-side phishing analysis, protected data storage, access controls, and monitored sessions. These are design decisions, not deployed features.

Architecture & data flow

Proposed design: browser → HTTPS web server → authenticated application API → database. The current site uses only the browser and GitHub Pages portions.

01 · FRONTEND👤 User BrowserHTML · CSS · JavaScriptImplemented
→HTTPS
02 · WEB SERVER🌐 Web DeliveryGitHub Pages today; reverse proxy in futureStatic hosting live
→API request
03 · APPLICATION⚙️ Analysis APIValidation · phishing model · access checksProposed
→Least privilege
04 · DATABASE🗄️ Protected StorageUsers · results · minimal audit logsProposed
🔒 Encryption in transit and at rest🪪 Authentication + secure sessions🛂 Role-based authorization🧹 Input validation + rate limits
NINE REQUIRED COMPONENTS

Security controls and responsibilities

Each component has a clear role in the design, with current functionality separated from planned functionality.

01

Frontend

Responsive pages, email input form, learning challenges, and result displays. Treat every input as untrusted.

Implemented
02

Web server

GitHub Pages currently hosts static files via HTTPS. A future reverse proxy could route API requests and apply traffic limits.

Static hosting implemented
03

Application layer

Future server-side API for phishing classification, validation, business rules, logging, and model inference.

Proposed
04

Database

Future database for account records and optional saved analyses, with minimal retention and restricted service credentials.

Proposed
05

Authentication

Future sign-in using strong password hashing, account protection, and optional multi-factor authentication.

Proposed
06

Authorization

Server-side checks ensure users can access only their own analyses; administrators receive limited, audited privileges.

Proposed
07

Encryption

HTTPS protects traffic to the published site today. Future sensitive records would also use encryption at rest and managed secrets.

HTTPS implemented · storage proposed
08

Session management

Future sessions would use Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies, short expiration times, and session invalidation on logout.

Proposed
09

Input validation

Future API validates email length and format, limits request size, escapes displayed content, and avoids executing pasted links or HTML.

Server-side controls proposed

Example: checking a suspicious email

  1. Submit: The user pastes a suspicious email into the frontend.
  2. Protect: HTTPS encrypts the request to the future API; rate limits and input validation reject unsafe or oversized requests.
  3. Analyze: The application layer runs the detection model and creates a risk explanation without opening links in the email.
  4. Control access: If saving is enabled, the server checks the user's identity and permission before writing an encrypted record.
  5. Respond: The frontend shows a risk score, warning signs, and safety guidance without rendering untrusted HTML.

Security principle: Do not store pasted email content by default. If saved analyses are added later, request consent and apply retention limits. This design also supports STRIDE mitigations for spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, and denial of service.

ASSIGNMENT 06 · COMPUTER SECURITY

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Security

Learn how untrusted input could change a web page and how PhishAware safely handles text submitted by visitors.

01 · SECURITY PROBLEM

Untrusted content can become executable code

If an application inserts user-supplied text into HTML without protection, the browser may interpret it as markup or JavaScript. This can lead to unwanted page changes, data exposure, or actions performed in a user's session.

Example: A malicious comment, profile field, or chatbot message displayed as HTML rather than plain text.

02 · SECURITY CONTROL

Validate input and encode output

Check input length and type, reject invalid data, and display user content using textContent instead of interpreting it with innerHTML. Use context-appropriate output encoding and sanitization when rich HTML is truly necessary.

03 · MITIGATION

Handle visitor messages safely

PhishAware's new practice area treats typed content as text. Production applications should also enforce validation on the server, sanitize permitted HTML, use a carefully configured Content Security Policy, and protect session cookies.

04 · SECURITY IMPROVEMENT

Lower the risk of script injection

Visitors can enter questions and profile information without those messages being interpreted as executable HTML in the protected display. This reduces a common XSS risk, but does not prove the whole website is free from vulnerabilities.

INTERACTIVE · SAFE XSS DEMONSTRATION

See input validation and safe output handling

Type a message or choose the harmless markup sample. The output should show the characters exactly as typed, not create a new HTML element. This demonstration does not execute injected scripts.

Network Identity & Security Lab

A hands-on investigation of network addressing, connectivity, routing, DNS, DHCP, and ARP using real macOS Terminal observations.

OBSERVED RESULTS · MACOS TERMINAL

Network configuration and DHCP

During the later tests, DHCP reported a /24 subnet mask (255.255.255.0), a 60-minute lease, and the local router serving as both default gateway and DNS resolver. The DHCP response was an ACK. No DNS servers were manually configured in Wi-Fi settings; macOS reported a DNS resolver automatically.

Network change note: An earlier configuration check showed a different private subnet and gateway. The later DHCP, traceroute, and ARP observations belong to the 192.168.1.0/24 network. Results from the two configurations are not treated as a single unchanged session.

Gateway ping · earlier network

4/4 received · 0% loss

Average RTT: 4.742 ms; range 3.649–6.684 ms.

Google ping · earlier network

Two tests · 0% loss

Average RTTs: 24.260 ms and 25.013 ms; TTL 106.

Router ping · later network

4/4 received · 0% loss

Average RTT: 26.708 ms; range 10.182–69.606 ms; TTL 64.

Traceroute comparison · five trials per destination

TrialGoogleKean University
1Reached at hop 6Last responding hop: 8
2Reached at hop 7Last responding hop: 8
3Destination responded at hop 6Last responding hop: 8
4Destination responded at hop 6Last responding hop: 8
5Reached at hop 6Last responding hop: 8

Google returned destination responses in all five trials, with slightly varying intermediate paths. Kean's destination did not respond within the 20-hop limit; hops 9–20 returned asterisks. This does not establish that the website was offline, because routers and servers may filter traceroute probes.

Topology diagrams are simplified from traceroute observations, not a complete map of physical network links.

ARP cache observations

The arp -a command returned 10 entries, including the local router, three devices labeled as iPhones, three incomplete entries, a broadcast entry, and a multicast entry. After pinging the router, the cache still showed 10 entries because its address mapping was already known. The ARP cache was not cleared during this test, so cache repopulation after deletion was not measured.

Conclusion

These tests demonstrate how IP configuration, DHCP, DNS, ICMP ping, traceroute, and ARP support network troubleshooting. Ping confirmed connectivity to tested destinations, traceroute revealed variable paths and nonresponsive hops, and ARP displayed local address mappings. Asterisks in traceroute and incomplete ARP entries must be interpreted cautiously rather than assumed to indicate an outage or attack.

LAB 1 · WEBSITE LABORATORY REPORT

1. Description

I investigated network identity, IP configuration, DHCP, DNS, connectivity, routing, and ARP on a macOS laptop using Terminal. My goal was to understand how devices communicate on a local network and across the Internet.

2. Procedure and Notes

I checked network interfaces with ifconfig, the gateway with route -n get default, DNS settings with networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi and scutil --dns, and DHCP with ipconfig getpacket en0. I ran ping -c 4 to the gateway, Google and a later router; traced routes to Google and Kean five times each using traceroute -m 20 -w 1; and viewed the ARP table using arp -a before and after router traffic.

Session note: The earlier IP/gateway tests and later DHCP/ARP tests were on different private networks. I did not deliberately change an IP address, renew a DHCP lease, or clear the ARP cache; those actions have no observed results to report.

3. Results and Reports

The result cards, traceroute comparison, and topology sketches above document my observations. In the later session, DHCP acknowledged a 60-minute lease with subnet mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway/DNS resolver 192.168.1.1. Ping tests showed 0% loss; Google was reached in all five traceroutes at 6–7 hops. Kean's destination did not reply within the 20-hop limit, although routers through hop 8 responded. The ARP cache showed ten entries before and after router traffic.

Answers to laboratory questions

IP: Windows ipconfig /all displays detailed adapter settings, ipconfig /release releases a DHCP lease, and ipconfig /renew requests renewal. macOS commands used in this lab provide comparable details. A subnet mask identifies the network portion of an IP address; the later /24 mask identifies the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet. I did not intentionally change and restore my IP address.

Ping: The first gateway's four RTTs were 4.419, 3.649, 6.684 and 4.216 ms (TTL 255). Google's first four were 12.466, 16.458, 12.413 and 55.702 ms (TTL 106). The later router's four were 69.606, 13.435, 13.609 and 10.182 ms (TTL 64). Replies and 0% loss confirmed that the tested destinations responded to ICMP probes.

Traceroute: Google reached the destination at hops 6, 7, 6, 6 and 6, with slightly different routes. Kean's last responding router was hop 8 in each trial; the destination was not confirmed within 20 hops. The largest observed RTTs were 20.709 ms in the Google trials and 47.468 ms in the Kean trials. Nonresponses do not necessarily mean a website is offline. Simplified topology sketches appear above.

ARP: arp -a displays the local ARP table. I observed ten entries, including the router, three iPhone-labeled devices, three incomplete entries, and broadcast/multicast entries. The table still had ten entries after pinging the router. Cache clearing and repopulation were not tested.

4. Reference and Acknowledgement

References: course Lab 1 instructions and my own macOS Terminal output. Utilities used: ifconfig, route, ping, traceroute, arp, networksetup, scutil and ipconfig. I acknowledge the course laboratory instructions for guiding the investigation.

🔒 This report is presented directly on my PhishAware website for link-based submission. Device MAC addresses and full ARP mappings are withheld for privacy. Original Terminal screenshots have not been embedded.

TECH 3498 · LAB 2

Network Configuration & Connectivity

Completed macOS practical — Anjolaoluwa Donna Dosu

Lab 2.1 A — Localhost and name resolution

Using macOS 15.6 (24G84) with administrator privileges, I ran ifconfig -a. Wi-Fi en0 was active with IPv4 192.168.1.221, subnet mask 255.255.255.0, broadcast 192.168.1.255, MTU 1500 and gateway 192.168.1.1. Loopback lo0 had 127.0.0.1 and ::1.

CommandReceived / sentLossAverage ms
ping -c 4 127.0.0.14/40%.112
ping6 -c 4 ::14/40%.231
ping -c 4 localhost4/40%.151
ping -c 4 me4/40%.239
ping -c 4 winserv4/40%9.764

Both loopback tests succeeded because they address the local host, but use different IP protocols (IPv4 TTL and IPv6 hop limit were 64). Timing differed slightly. localhost resolved to 127.0.0.1 through local name resolution.

Hosts file

I inspected /private/etc/hosts using sudo nano. Existing mappings were 127.0.0.1 localhost, 255.255.255.255 broadcasthost and ::1 localhost. Comments beginning with # document configuration and are ignored by the resolver. I backed up the file and temporarily added 192.168.1.1 winserv and 192.168.1.221 me. Both names resolved correctly. The gateway response took longer because it traversed the local network. I removed the two entries after testing.

A normal user cannot directly edit a properly protected hosts file. Incorrect permissions or a vulnerable privileged application could allow unauthorized changes that redirect users to malicious websites. Least privilege and file-integrity monitoring reduce this risk.

DNS cache

I ran sudo killall -INFO mDNSResponder and inspected unified logs with log show --last 5m --predicate 'process == "mDNSResponder"' --info. Logs showed completed DNS queries, resolver activity and no logged errors or faults in the inspected interval. Modern macOS privacy redaction prevented obtaining a complete readable DNS cache listing.

Lab 2.1 B — Nslookup and Netstat

I consulted man nslookup and used interactive set all to inspect the current DNS servers (IPv4 192.168.1.1 and an IPv6 resolver, redacted). DNS port 53, query type A, recursion enabled and three retries were reported. The server command changes the default server; set all displays the current settings.

Netstat displays socket and network statistics. On macOS, verbose socket output (netstat -anv) can expose process identifiers; lsof directly associates sockets with processes. I used sudo lsof -iTCP.

15 LISTEN entries and 22 ESTABLISHED entries were recorded. These are file-descriptor rows, not necessarily unique connections. Listening services included launchd (screen sharing), Kerberos, MySQL, rapportd, Control Center and a local Node development server. Established entries included browser HTTPS, Apple identity services, Mail IMAPS and local Node/browser communication. Listening sockets await connections; established sockets represent connected endpoints.

Lab 2.2 A — IPv6 and Wireshark

Windows netsh was skipped because this is macOS. The en0 interface had a link-local fe80::/64 address, a secured global autoconfigured address and a temporary global autoconfigured address (full addresses withheld for privacy). lo0 had ::1/128 and a link-local address. Other interfaces included peer-to-peer and tunnel interfaces.

I installed Wireshark 4.6.10 and ChmodBPF to resolve capture permissions. I started a Wi-Fi capture on en0 and ran ping6 -c 4 using my link-local address with %en0. Four replies were received with zero loss and an average of 0.328 ms.

sudo ifconfig en0 inet6 2001:db8:1234:5678::2 prefixlen 64 alias
ifconfig en0

The documentation address appeared with prefix length 64. Using the ipv6 display filter, I observed 7,524 of 8,209 Wi-Fi packets, including TCP, UDP, TLS and ICMPv6 neighbor discovery. No echo packets matched on en0 because the self-ping was handled locally. I switched to lo0 and used the filter icmpv6.type == 128 || icmpv6.type == 129. The repeated ping produced four echo requests and four echo replies, sequence numbers 0–3, hop limit 64 and captured frame length 60 bytes. Both source and destination were the local IPv6 address.

sudo ifconfig en0 inet6 2001:db8:1234:5678::2 -alias
ifconfig en0

The final output confirmed removal of the temporary address, preservation of the original addresses and active Wi-Fi. Captures were stopped and saved locally; raw packet captures are not published for privacy.

Practical screenshot evidence

Selected original Wireshark screenshots, cropped and redacted for privacy.

Conclusion

I learned to troubleshoot name resolution, inspect TCP connections, configure IPv6 temporarily, and select the correct capture interface. I resolved capture permissions and the missing echo packets and restored the original network configuration. DNS logging limitations were documented rather than treating an incomplete cache listing as successful.

TECH 3498 · LAB 3

Network Transport and Applications

macOS practical · November 24, 2026

3.1 A — ARP and ICMP

I inspected the ARP cache using arp -a, cleared four entries using sudo arp -d -a, and captured traffic on Wi-Fi en0. Running ping -c 4 192.168.1.1 produced four requests and four replies, zero loss, TTL 64 and average RTT 9.141 ms. Wireshark displayed 43 ARP and 8 ICMP packets. The packet list, protocol tree and raw bytes panes show packet summaries, decoded fields and hexadecimal data respectively.

ARP request 13: Ethernet destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff appears before source in the first six bytes; EtherType 0x0806; Ethernet header 14 bytes. ARP fields: Ethernet hardware type 1, IPv4 protocol 0x0800, hardware length 6, protocol length 4, opcode 1, sender IP 192.168.1.1, target IP 192.168.1.220 and populated sender/target hardware fields. Reply 183 (a separate exchange responding to 181) used opcode 2 and unicast addressing. Both frames were 42 bytes. ICMP echo requests/replies were packets 753/754, 756/757, 761/762 and 811/812.

DNS and UDP

nslookup kean.edu returned 131.125.16.38. The first DNS packet (8) queried clientservices.googleapis.com: UDP source 8946, destination 53, length 55, checksum 0x4a30 (unverified). Kean query 981 used source 61240, destination 53, length 34, checksum 0xa196 (unverified); response 982 returned the IPv4 address. Filter: dns.qry.name == "kean.edu".

TCP and Telnet

The ARP cache repopulated with five entries and was cleared again. Telnet was installed using Homebrew. telnet obi2.kean.edu timed out. Eleven SYN packets (one initial and ten retransmissions) were captured; no SYN-ACK was observed. First Telnet packet 303: source 56924, destination 23, header 44 bytes, frame 78 bytes, sequence and acknowledgment 0 (relative), window 65535, checksum 0x0c7f (unverified), no payload. Remote login and passwd inspection were not performed.

TCPUDP
Connection-oriented; sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and variable header (minimum 20 bytes)Connectionless; no built-in acknowledgment or retransmission; fixed 8-byte header
Telnet, SSH, HTTPSObserved DNS queries

3.2 A — File transfer and HTTPS

SSH to obi2.kean.edu on port 22 timed out. SFTP upload, remote directory listing, permissions and account-file inspection could not be performed. Traditional FTP uses separate control and data connections and is normally unencrypted; SFTP transfers files over encrypted SSH, usually port 22. A campus network or authorized VPN may be needed; the exact cause was not verified.

Both the main and personal web pages returned 403 Forbidden. A fresh curl -Iv --connect-timeout 10 https://obi2.kean.edu/ connected to 131.125.16.42:443, verified the certificate and negotiated TLS 1.2 (ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384). Apache returned HTTP/1.1 403. Unlike plaintext HTTP, HTTPS protects HTTP messages inside TLS. The filtered capture contained 23 packets out of 1,827, zero dropped. TCP handshake: 278 SYN, 280 SYN-ACK, 281 ACK. First packet 278: source 56938, destination 443, header 44 bytes, window 65535, checksum 0xc782 (unverified). TLS Client Hello, Server Hello, certificate, encrypted application data and connection termination were observed.

3.2 B — Email communication and security

Server-based mail and spoofing tests were blocked by the SSH timeout; no message or header comparison was performed. In principle, a forged From address can mislead recipients; Received headers and SPF, DKIM and DMARC results can help assess authenticity. Gmail Last account activity showed 0 minutes ago and Browser (Chrome). Google Security Checkup provides device, third-party access and security settings review; individual device and application details were not verified.

Captures were stopped and saved locally. No remote configuration was changed. Raw captures and private account details are not published.

Port Scanning and System Vulnerability

Lab 4.1 — Steps 1–5: Environment and installation

I used my Apple Silicon Mac with administrator access and installed Nmap through Homebrew after the initial command returned “command not found.” I used Terminal instead of Zenmap; the five Zenmap views are Nmap Output, Ports/Hosts, Topology, Host Details and Scans. Wireshark initially captured on Wi-Fi (en0).

brew install nmap
nmap --version

192.168.1.221

Step 6 — Scan my own computer

The worksheet gives -sn as an intensive scan example, but it is host discovery only. I ran host discovery, service detection and an intensive scan separately.

nmap -sn 192.168.1.221
1 host up; 0.04 seconds
nmap -sV 192.168.1.221
88/tcp open tcpwrapped
3306/tcp open mysql (unauthorized)
5000/tcp open rtsp
5900/tcp open Apple remote desktop VNC
7000/tcp open rtsp
995 closed; 18.96 seconds
sudo nmap -A 192.168.1.221
3306, 5000, 5900, 7000 open; 996 closed
41.83 seconds

Ports 5000 and 7000 responded with AirTunes HTTP/RTSP 403 Forbidden. Port 5900 reported VNC protocol 3.889. Some service fingerprints were unrecognized and two scripts did not complete. The initial Wi-Fi capture showed unrelated HTTPS traffic, so I switched to loopback (lo0) for the self-scan.

sudo nmap -sS 192.168.1.221
4 open ports: 3306, 5000, 5900, 7000
996 closed ports; 0.06 seconds

The initial SYN packets used source port 49384. Open ports returned SYN-ACK; closed ports returned RST-ACK. The loopback capture could not be saved, but these screenshots preserve the observed results.

Steps 7–8 — Subnet discovery and ARP broadcasts

sudo nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24
256 IP addresses; 14 hosts up; 4.56 seconds
Repeat: 15 hosts up; 3.91 seconds

Discovered addresses (192.168.1.x): 1, 100, 101, 102, 103, 153, 157, 170, 187, 191, 192, 193, 194, 221. The repeat also discovered .173. The number of responding devices can change over time.

ARP broadcasts ask which device owns a local IPv4 address so that its hardware address can be learned. The destination broadcast address is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. Both the router and Mac sent requests. Frames 424 and 425 occurred at 14.986433 and 14.986443 seconds, only 10 microseconds apart. The capture also contained background ARP traffic.

Steps 9–11 — TCP connect scan

nmap -sT 192.168.1.1
53/tcp open domain
80/tcp open http
443/tcp open https
997 closed (conn-refused)
1.73 seconds

The default scan tested 1,000 TCP ports, not all 65,536 port numbers. A TCP connect scan uses the operating system to establish a connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK); closed ports generally respond with RST-ACK. The expected gateway packets did not appear under the Wireshark filters, so the capture count and completed handshake could not be verified. This is a limitation, not an observed handshake.

Steps 12–15 — SYN scan and packet comparison

sudo nmap -sS 192.168.1.1
53, 80, 443 open
997 closed (reset)
0.35 seconds

Both scans found the same three open ports. The SYN scan was approximately 4.94 times faster. Wireshark captured 24,646 packets; three matched tcp.port == 80, with no dropped packets.

FrameTime (s)DirectionFlags
54418.929049Mac:34419 → gateway:80SYN
55418.933631Gateway:80 → Mac:34419SYN-ACK
56118.933760Mac:34419 → gateway:80RST

The scanner reset the connection instead of completing the three-way handshake.

Step 16 — Operating system fingerprinting

sudo nmap -O 192.168.1.1
Running: Linux 5.X, MikroTik RouterOS 7.X
OS details: Linux 5.0–5.14; MikroTik RouterOS 7.2–7.5
Network distance: 1 hop
2.19 seconds

These are fingerprint estimates, not verified router firmware. The intensive scan of my Mac estimated macOS 12 Monterey, but Lynis identified macOS 15.6 Sequoia (kernel 24.6.0). This demonstrates the limitations of fingerprint-based detection.

4.2 — Vulnerability research

Research topic: Windows Server 2019 vulnerabilities. Search results included NIST NVD and the Irish NCSC advisory. Google hit count and exact top-five Google domains were not verified. CVE-2025-29824 affects Windows Server 2019 and 2022, among other systems; it is a privilege escalation issue in the Windows Common Log File System driver, published April 8, 2025 (CVSS 7.8). NCSC advisory.

CVE Details vendor and weighted-average pages returned HTTP 403; requested rankings and vulnerability/product ratios could not be verified. An alternative vendor comparison lists Linux, Microsoft, Google, Oracle and IBM, but is not the requested CVE Details ranking. Alternative comparison.

CVE identifiers uniquely reference publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. The current CVE portal is CVE.org. The exact count for Microsoft Windows 2022 Server was not verified.

CVE-2022-30216: Windows Server Service Tampering Vulnerability, published July 12, 2022. CVSS v3.1 base score 8.8 (High), as reported by Rapid7 and Vulners. NVD page did not yield readable data; impact and exploitability subscores were not independently verified. A Rapid7 vulnerability reference exists, but a dedicated exploit module and its severity were not confirmed. Microsoft advisory · NVD · Rapid7 · Vulners.

Lynis system audit

Version 3.1.7; macOS 15.6, kernel 24.6.0, arm64. The privileged audit was canceled after an ownership safety check; the non-privileged audit completed without modifying permissions. Five listed privileged tests were skipped. Hardening index: 64/100; 170 tests; 18 suggestions; two plugins; zero final summary warnings. Individual checks flagged printer and home directory permissions. Firewall was reported inactive and independently confirmed disabled using the macOS firewall status command. FileVault was enabled. No package audit, intrusion detection or malware scanner was detected by Lynis; this does not prove built-in macOS protections are absent.

Recommendations: enable the macOS firewall, review listening services and sharing settings, update software, review permissions and printing exposure, and verify built-in security protections. Linux-specific suggestions require macOS applicability review. Findings are configuration weaknesses, not confirmed CVE exploits.

Additional scanner: Nessus uses vulnerability checks to identify exposed services, missing patches and misconfigurations. Installation and scanning were skipped; no Nessus results are claimed. Nessus Essentials. No security settings were changed for the audit.

ASSIGNMENT 7 · CYBERSECURITY RESEARCH & FILM

Protecting Website Availability

Investigating DoS and DDoS traffic using public intrusion-detection data, and telling the story through a short cybersecurity film.

Research question

Can data-driven methods help identify abnormal network traffic associated with DoS and DDoS attacks before website availability is seriously affected?

Objective: Compare benign and malicious traffic, identify predictive flow characteristics, and evaluate defensive detection approaches.

DoS vs. DDoS

DoS: An attempt to exhaust a service's resources or capacity from one primary source.

DDoS: A coordinated disruption using many distributed sources, which can be harder to filter using simple source-based controls.

Both threaten availability, one of the three core cybersecurity principles.

Public research dataset: CIC-IDS2017

Selected source: CIC-IDS2017 on Kaggle, originally developed by the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity. It contains labeled network-flow records, including benign activity, DDoS, and several DoS variants.

Labels: BENIGN, DDoS, DoS Hulk, DoS GoldenEye, DoS slowloris, and DoS Slowhttptest, among other attack categories. Candidate features: Flow Duration, Total Fwd Packets, Total Backward Packets, Flow Bytes/s, Flow Packets/s, packet lengths, and inter-arrival times (feature availability depends on dataset file).

Research scope: Only BENIGN, DDoS, and DoS-labeled records are considered for the binary comparison. Other attacks are excluded rather than incorrectly treated as normal traffic.

Normal network traffic

Ordinary traffic often follows a mix of user-driven requests, response packets, varying session durations, and changing packet sizes. Its volume varies with legitimate activity, so high traffic alone is not proof of an attack.

Attack-associated behavior

Possible indicators include sustained spikes in flows or packets, unusually short gaps between requests, many similar connections, high forward-to-backward packet imbalance, and bursts from multiple sources. No single feature proves an attack.

Traffic visualization — conceptual example

The chart below is illustrative, not measured from CIC-IDS2017. It demonstrates a potential change in traffic volume; it must not be presented as an experimental result.

Volume comparison: The hypothesis is that attack intervals may contain a higher concentration of flows, packets, or bytes than comparable benign intervals. The actual size of any difference must be calculated from the selected dataset.

Preprocessing and detection methodology

  1. Load the downloaded CIC-IDS2017 CSV files and standardize column names.
  2. Retain BENIGN, DDoS, and DoS categories; remove duplicate records and replace infinite values with missing values.
  3. Convert numerical features, inspect missing values, and summarize distributions by traffic class.
  4. Compare flow rate, packet rate, packet counts, and duration with charts and class-specific statistics.
  5. Use a stratified train/test split and a median-imputation + random-forest classification pipeline, with a fixed random seed.
  6. Report precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix, including false negatives and false positives.

Download reproducible Python analysis script · Analysis instructions

Interpretation and availability

Precision describes how often an alert really corresponds to attack traffic. Recall measures how many actual attacks were caught. F1 balances the two. The confusion matrix reveals missed attacks and false alarms.

Detection can support alerting, rate limiting, traffic filtering, and capacity planning, but detection alone does not guarantee uninterrupted service.

Results, limitations, and next steps

Status: Dataset and reproducible analysis method selected. No measured model scores are claimed yet; run the included script on downloaded CSV files to generate results and replace this note.

Limitations: dataset age, possible class imbalance, lab-generated traffic, concept drift, and differences between flow classification and live website monitoring.

Next: evaluate unseen time periods, examine false negatives, and compare a baseline threshold detector with the trained model.

AI Movie: PhishAware — Under Attack

This short AI-generated cybersecurity movie was created using Google Flow and edited in CapCut. It features two cybersecurity analysts investigating suspicious network traffic and identifying a possible DDoS attack.

Final AI Movie: A 16-second animated cybersecurity film featuring AI-generated characters, spoken dialogue, and an educational DDoS attack scenario.

Research conclusion

Network-flow features provide a reasonable basis for investigating abnormal behavior linked to DoS and DDoS attacks. A defensible conclusion about how well a detector works requires evaluation on real labeled records. Combining traffic monitoring, careful classification, and layered protections can help security teams respond to threats against website availability.

Safety: This project uses publicly available research data and offline analysis only. No traffic attacks were performed.

Sources: CIC-IDS2017 (Kaggle) · Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity

TECH 3498 · ASSIGNMENT 9

Research and Model Comparison

Kean University · Information Technology and Cybersecurity

Research objective

Compare ten baseline classifiers, optimize SVM, and evaluate a weighted hybrid for phishing email detection. The study investigates the trade-off between missed phishing messages and false alarms.

Read final research paper (PDF) Download research notebook

17,521 emails

10,978 safe; 6,543 phishing.

5,000 features

TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams; fitted on training data only.

12 configurations

Ten baseline models, optimized SVM and PhishAware Hybrid.

Methodology

Training: 12,264; validation: 2,628; testing: 2,629. Python and Google Colab were used to evaluate Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM, KNN, Naive Bayes, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost.

Seven SVM regularization values were evaluated. C = 0.5 achieved validation F1 of 97.02%. The hybrid used sigmoid-calibrated SVM, Logistic Regression and XGBoost; 324 weight/threshold configurations were compared on validation data.

Proposed hybrid

Score = 0.40 × SVM probability + 0.30 × Logistic Regression probability + 0.30 × XGBoost probability. Classify as phishing when score ≥ 0.45. Validation F1: 97.15%.

Kaggle dataset

Research findings and reproducibility

Baseline SVM achieved 98.21% test accuracy and 97.61% F1. The hybrid detected 960 of 982 phishing emails, compared with 958 for baseline SVM. See Assignment 10 for the complete evaluation. To reproduce the experiment, open the linked notebook in Google Colab, obtain the linked Kaggle dataset, and execute the cells in order using the specified training, validation and test partitions.

IEEE research paper

Download final results CSV

Key finding

The hybrid detected 960 phishing emails versus 958 for baseline SVM, reducing missed phishing emails from 24 to 22 (8.33% relative reduction). False positives increased from 23 to 33. Hybrid accuracy was 97.91%, F1 was 97.22%, and ROC-AUC was 0.9975. Baseline SVM remains the strongest overall model by accuracy and F1.

Limitations and future work

One public dataset, text-only features, no statistical significance testing, and no external validation. Future work includes additional datasets, email headers, sender authentication, URL and attachment analysis, cost-sensitive optimization and deployment. The existing website analyzer is rule-based, not a deployed trained classifier.

Conclusion and supporting files

The baseline SVM is the strongest overall classifier by accuracy and F1. The hybrid offers a modest improvement in phishing recall at the cost of additional false alarms; its advantage is not established on external datasets.
